Title: Large Language Models as Simulative Agents for Neurodivergent Adult Psychometric Profiles
Snippet: To ensure an adequate variety of instruments suitable for simulation, four standardized psychometric tests for the adult population were selected. Two of these assess high-functioning autism: the Ritvo Autism Asperger Diagnostic Scale-Revised (RAADS-R) and the Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ). For the evaluation of adult ADHD, the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) and the Barkley Adult ADHD Rating Scale-IV (BAARS-IV) were chosen, the latter including a specific subscale for Sluggish Cognitive Tempo (SCT). All four tests were used in Italian translation form. 

The RAADS-R, developed by Ritvo and colleagues [33], was designed to fill the gap in screening tools for adults with high-functioning autism. It comprises 80 items divided into four subscales: social relatedness, circumscribed interests, language, and sensorimotor functioning. Unlike traditional Likert-type instruments, its four response options (0 to 3) refer not to behavioral frequency but to the time period in which behaviors occurred ("never," "only before age 16," "both now and before 16," "only now"). While the scale shows high sensitivity, specificity, and test-retest reliability, self-awareness and interpretation of questions may affect accuracy, particularly among adults who tend to mask or minimize symptoms. 

The Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ) [34] is a self-report screening tool developed to assess the presence and degree of autistic traits in intellectually typical adults. It consists of 50 items grouped into five domains: social skill, attention switching, attention to detail, communication, and imagination. Responses are rated on a four-point Likert scale, and higher total scores indicate a greater presence of autistic traits. Although not diagnostic, the AQ demonstrates good construct validity, discriminant power, and high test-retest reliability across both clinical and non-clinical populations. In this study was used the original scoring procedure proposed by Baron-Cohen and colleagues [34], each item is assigned a binary value: one point for an "autistic" response and zero for a "non-autistic" one.

Title: Neuropsychological Assessment in Autism Spectrum Disorder
Snippet: Many domains of neuropsychological functioning, including intelligence and executive function, are impacted by attentional capacity. While previous versions of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) did not allow for a dual diagnosis of autism and ADHD, attentional difficulties are now recognized as one of the most common comorbidities, with ADHD prevalence in people with ASD falling in the 40-70% range [42]. Those with more severe forms of ASD have been found to present with more significant deficits in attention and behavior regulation [43]. The co-occurrence of ASD and attention problems is also associated with decreased adaptive skills [44], making the assessment and treatment of ADHD symptoms in this population essential for improving long-term outcomes.

In order to better understand the unique neuropsychological assessment needs of individuals on the autism spectrum with and without attention deficits, a recent study by Ng et al. administered standardized assessments of intellectual, attentional, social, and executive function to participants with ASD, ADHD, and comorbid ASD + ADHD and found differing symptom profiles depending on domain and informant [45•]. While parent-report on the Conners 3 [46], a questionnaire that measures domains such as attention and hyperactivity, differentiated individuals with ASD from those with ADHD or ASD + ADHD, an objective attention task (i.e., the Conners Continuous Performance Test, 2nd Edition [47]) did not [45•]. Conversely, objective assessment of social functioning and affect (i.e., NEPSY-II Affect Recognition and Theory of Mind tasks [38]) better differentiated both ASD groups from the ADHD alone group, with the ASD groups showing greater deficits in social perception, while parentreport of social skills on the Social Responsiveness Scale, 2nd Edition (SRS-2 [48]), did not [45•]. Interestingly, no significant group differences were identified related to executive function as measured by the D-KEFS Tower Test or the Children's Category Test [45•]. This study emphasizes the benefits of integrating information from multiple sources to differentially assess ASD and attention problems, as well as the co-occurrence of the two. Title: Physical Aggression Toward Others and Self: Correlates in Autism, Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, and Population-Based Child Samples
Snippet: The autism and ADHD samples comprised 2,492 children (1,436 with autism, 747 with ADHD-C, and 309 with ADHD-I), 2 to 17 years of age, evaluated in a psychiatry and behavioral health diagnostic clinic. Children were classified with ADHD-I if the median hyperactiveimpulsive rating was less than often a problem. All children in the ADHD group scored below the autism range on the CASD. Children in the autism sample had a DSM-IV or DSM-5 diagnosis of autism (ie, autistic disorder, Asperger's disorder, or autism spectrum disorder) and a score in the autism range on the CASD. Title: The relationship between executive function, neurodevelopmental disorder traits, and academic achievement in university students
Snippet: This was an online study which required the use of an internet-capable device and an internet connection. Data were collected across two academic years; 2020-2021 and 2021-2022. Self-report data was obtained from four questionnaires. Executive functioning was determined by scores on the Amsterdam Executive Function Inventory (AEFI; Van der Elst et al., 2012), consisting of 13 items assessing executive function using a three-point scale consisting of not true (1), partly true (2), or true (3). This scale was chosen over laboratory methods due to the convenience of it being able to be completed by a large sample, and it may also provide a better insight into executive functions in everyday life rather than laboratorybased methods which may lack ecological validity somewhat (Leonard and Hill, 2015). 

ASD traits were measured using the Autism Quotient (AQ; Baron-Cohen et al., 2001), which consists of 50 items regarding autism-typical behaviors on a four-point scale consisting of definitely agree (1), slightly agree (2), slightly disagree (3), or definitely disagree (4). Definitely agree and slightly agree responses were scored 1 point on autism-typical items such as "I prefer to do things the same way over and over again." There were 26 reverse scored items, such as "I prefer to do things with others rather than on my own, " where slightly disagree and definitely disagree were scored 1 point. 

ADHD traits were measured using the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS; Kessler et al., 2005), which has 18 items relating to ADHD traits. Participants indicated how often each item occurs in their life on a five-point scale from never (1) to very often (5). DCD traits were measured using the Adult DCD Checklist (ADC; Kirby et al., 2010), which has 30 items relating to motor coordination. This measure is divided into two sections; childhood (10 items) and present time (20 items). Participants indicated how often these items apply to them, on a four-point scale from never (1) to always (4). Responses on all measures were scored summed to provide a total score.

Summary and clinical context
Current adult autism diagnostic tools can detect autistic traits and impairments, but they often cannot reliably separate autism from ADHD when executive dysfunction and social difficulties coexist because many symptoms overlap and the discriminant signal is weak or domain-specific rather than categorical. Convergent evidence from clinician-administered and self-report instruments indicates substantial ASD–ADHD symptom overlap in adults, with differences that are frequently quantitative and profile-based, which challenges single-test, binary diagnostic certainty. In practice, reliable distinction typically requires combining autism-specific and ADHD-specific assessments and emphasizing social-cognitive and adaptive-functioning evidence alongside executive measures. <cite id="e0a295aa-0">Adults with ADHD show significant ASD symptoms on ADOS-2 and item-level similarities suggest differences of degree rather than kind, underscoring the need to assess full ASD symptom domains in ADHD</cite> <cite id="e0a295aa-1">AQ and ADHD symptom scores in adults are not correlated within ASD and ADHD groups, suggesting overlap at the dimensional level rather than purely genetic comorbidity</cite> <cite id="e0a295aa-2">AQ total scores tend to be higher in ASD than ADHD, but ROC-based cutoffs yield around 73% correct classifications, limiting clinical differentiation</cite> <cite id="e0a295aa-4">Combining emotion-related, attention, and AQ/empathy measures discriminates ADHD, ASD, and ADHD+ASD better than single tools</cite>.

What the overlap looks like in adults
Adults with ADHD frequently endorse autistic-like social and repetitive behaviors, and adults with ASD commonly show ADHD-like inattention and impulsivity, making boundary crossing common in clinical presentations with overlapping executive dysfunction and social difficulties. <cite id="e0a295aa-0">ADHD adults exhibit ASD symptoms that fall between ASD and neurotypical groups on ADOS-2, with item-level analyses indicating more similarities than clear qualitative differences</cite> <cite id="e0a295aa-1">Adults with ASD show ADHD symptoms and vice versa; correlations between AQ and ADHD symptom scores are absent within groups, implying dimensional overlap rather than simple comorbidity</cite> <cite id="e0a295aa-3">In a clinical adult sample, subjective ASD and ADHD symptoms overlapped significantly even without formal dual diagnosis, with no correlation between AQ and CAARS</cite>. Executive dysfunction is elevated in both populations, complicating interpretation of EF-related items and tasks. <cite id="5a324636-0">Adults with ADHD show elevated behavioral regulation difficulties and everyday dysexecutive symptoms, paralleling ADHD youth; rigorous ASD samples often fail to control for co-occurring ADHD, obscuring autism-specific EF patterns</cite> <cite id="5a324636-1">Adult ASD performance on executive tasks and self-/informant-reported dysexecutive symptoms should be compared to age- and IQ-matched controls while removing ADHD confounds to clarify autism-specific EF profiles</cite>.

Performance of current autism diagnostic tools vs ADHD
- ADOS-2 (Clinician-administered): Differentiates group-level but with overlap; item-level convergence suggests careful use in ADHD adults. <cite id="e0a295aa-0">ADHD adults show ASD symptom profiles on ADOS-2 Module 4 that are higher than controls but lower than ASD, with item analyses indicating similarities that may reflect degree rather than quality</cite>. While ADOS-2 reliably detects ASD features, its discriminant power against ADHD is limited by shared social-related behaviors and overlapping item domains; thus, clinicians should add targeted history and social-cognitive tasks to reduce ambiguity. <cite id="e0a295aa-0">Differences may be quantitative, emphasizing the importance of full ASD symptom assessment in ADHD</cite>.
- AQ (Autism-Spectrum Quotient): Useful for screening autistic traits, but alone it has modest discriminant validity for ASD vs ADHD. <cite id="e0a295aa-2">All but one AQ subscore was higher in ASD than ADHD; a cut-off of 26 yielded 73% correct classifications, indicating limited clinical utility for differentiation</cite>. AQ can still inform risk and profile (e.g., social skill deficits), but comorbidities and masking/minimization affect accuracy. <cite id="5a324636-4">AQ shows good construct validity and high test–retest reliability and is sensitive to autistic traits; however, self-awareness and interpretation may impact accuracy, especially when adults mask symptoms</cite>.
- Trait-based discriminant models: Combining autism-related and ADHD-related dimensions improves separation. <cite id="e0a295aa-4">BAARS-IV (ADHD), AQ (autism), and EQ (empathy) differentiate ASD vs ADHD and co-occurring cases; ASD vs ADHD+ASD discrimination involved BAARS-IV current and EQ; affective lability (ALS) subscales, past BAARS-IV, and AQ differentiated ADHD from ASD</cite> <cite id="5a324636-3">Trait dimensions—current impulsivity, attention to detail, imagination, and empathy—discriminate ADHD, ASD, and co-occurring groups better than categorical scores</cite>. These findings support using multi-trait composites (e.g., social-empathy plus executive/attention) rather than relying on a single autism tool.

Executive dysfunction and social-cognitive contributions
Executive dysfunction overlaps ASD and ADHD, but domain-specific tasks and informants shift discriminant signals. Studies emphasize that objective social-cognitive tasks often better separate ASD from ADHD than self/parent reports, whereas EF tests may show minimal group differences, underscoring the need to weigh informant bias and ecological validity. <cite id="5a324636-2">Objective social functioning and affect tasks (e.g., affect recognition and theory of mind) differentiated ASD from ADHD groups more than parent reports; parent Conners-3 differentiated ASD from ADHD/ASD+ADHD, while the Conners CPT did not; EF tasks (D-KEFS Tower, Children’s Category Test) showed no significant group differences</cite>. Executive dysfunction in adult ADHD and ASD co-occurrence alters adaptive functioning and attentional profiles, requiring integration of neurocognitive and adaptive measures. <cite id="5a324636-0">ADHD symptoms and core ASD characteristics both contribute to BRIEF domains (inhibition, shift, emotional control), suggesting ADHD-like EF difficulties can elevate in adults with ASD, complicating autism-specific EF conclusions</cite> <cite id="5a324636-2">ADHD prevalence in ASD ranges 40–70%; more severe ASD shows greater attention/behavior regulation deficits, with co-occurring ADHD linked to decreased adaptive skills; integrating multiple assessments is essential</cite>.

Practical implications for distinguishing autism from ADHD in adults
- Reliability with overlapping EF and social difficulties: When executive dysfunction and social difficulties co-occur, autism-specific tools (ADOS-2, AQ, RAADS-R) have useful but limited standalone discriminant validity versus ADHD; clinicians should interpret higher AQ and social-related ADOS items cautiously in ADHD-suspect adults, because overlapping symptoms can inflate autism trait scores without ASD-level social-cognitive impairment. <cite id="e0a295aa-0">ADHD adults exhibit significant ASD symptoms, suggesting that elevated social/communication items may reflect shared dysfunction</cite> <cite id="e0a295aa-2">AQ alone yields about 73% correct classifications between ASD and ADHD, indicating limited standalone reliability for diagnosis</cite>.
- Recommended multi-domain strategy: Combine autism-focused social-cognitive and adaptive-functioning evidence with ADHD-focused attention/impulsivity evidence. Objective social-cognitive tasks and informant triangulation (clinician, observer, self-report) improve discrimination. <cite id="5a324636-2">Objective social-affect tasks differentiate ASD from ADHD better than parent-report alone; parent ADHD questionnaires can differentiate ASD vs ADHD/ASD+ADHD, but objective attention tasks often fail to</cite> <cite id="e0a295aa-4">Incorporating affect (ALS) subscales with ADHD ratings and AQ/EQ improves classification of ADHD vs ASD and co-occurrence</cite>.
- Use composite thresholds and watch for comorbidity: Because trait dimensions (impulsivity, attention to detail, empathy/imagination) carry the strongest discriminant signal, clinicians can apply empirically informed composites (e.g., high AQ plus low empathy and high ADHD-attention/impulsivity) to flag co-occurrence and schedule full diagnostic consensus. <cite id="5a324636-3">Empathy, current impulsivity, attention to detail, and imagination distinguish ADHD, ASD, and co-occurrence</cite> <cite id="e0a295aa-4">AQ plus EQ and ADHD symptom time-course differentiate ASD vs ADHD and co-occurrence</cite>.
- Case-specific interpretation: In adults where EF deficits are prominent, consider ADHD-like patterns of attentional switching and inhibitory control masking autistic social-cognitive profiles, or conversely, autistic social-cognitive deficits inflating ADHD ratings; multi-informant history and functional adaptive outcomes help resolve ambiguity. <cite id="5a324636-0">ADHD-like EF difficulties are common in adults and can mimic or confound autism-specific EF impairments if comorbid ADHD is not rigorously evaluated</cite> <cite id="5a324636-2">Co-occurrence is common and linked to decreased adaptive skills; integrating information from multiple sources is necessary</cite>.

Evidence boundaries and open questions
- Pediatric CASD-5 performance does not directly translate to adult certainty: CASD-5 shows near-ceiling accuracy and high agreement with ADI-R/ADI in children and differentiates autism from other disorders, including ADHD, but adult samples show overlapping symptom profiles and EF confounds; adult validation and ROC data for CASD-5 vs ADHD are limited in the retrieved evidence. <cite id="b1307cb9-0">In standardization, CASD identified children with and without autism with 99.5% accuracy and differentiated autism from other disorders, including ADHD, with diagnostic agreement 93–98% with ADI-R/CSI</cite> <cite id="b1307cb9-2">All children in ADHD samples scored below autism range on CASD; most autistic children had ADHD symptoms</cite>. Clinicians should treat adult CASD-5/ADOS-2 discriminant claims cautiously and integrate ADHD-specific measures.
- Adaptive functioning and functional networks: Incorporating adaptive functioning and functional network biomarkers can improve differential sensitivity, but field evidence is still emergent. <cite id="b1307cb9-3">Community diagnoses used ADOS/ADI-R and ADHD confirmed with parent/teacher/clinic scales; network integrity analyses integrated executive and clinical measures</cite>.

Bottom line
- Can current adult autism diagnostic tools reliably distinguish autism from ADHD with overlapping EF and social difficulties? Alone, no. Autism tools (ADOS-2, AQ, RAADS-R) detect relevant impairments but show modest discriminant validity against ADHD when executive dysfunction and social difficulties overlap; relying on a single tool risks misclassification. <cite id="e0a295aa-0">ADHD adults show ASD-like profiles on ADOS-2 with item-level convergence</cite> <cite id="e0a295aa-2">AQ ROC accuracy around 73% for ASD vs ADHD suggests limited standalone differentiation</cite> <cite id="5a324636-2">Objective social tasks better separate ASD from ADHD than EF tests, highlighting domain specificity</cite>.
- What works: Multi-informant, multi-domain differential assessment that integrates autism-specific social-cognitive and adaptive-functioning evidence with ADHD-specific attention/impulsivity and executive measures; use empirically derived composite dimensions (AQ/EQ with BAARS/ASRS and affect/impulsivity subscales) to flag overlap and guide consensus diagnosis. <cite id="e0a295aa-4">AQ/EQ plus ADHD symptom measures and affect/impulsivity subscales discriminate ADHD, ASD, and co-occurrence</cite> <cite id="5a324636-3">Empathy, impulsivity, attention to detail, and imagination are key discriminant traits</cite>. Clinicians should set expectations that reliable categorical separation is uncommon in overlap-rich cases and should prioritize longitudinal history, functional outcomes, and targeted neuropsychological/social-cognitive testing to reduce ambiguity. <cite id="5a324636-2">Integrating multiple assessment sources is essential when ASD and ADHD co-occur</cite> <cite id="e0a295aa-1">Symptom overlap at dimensional level argues for cautious interpretation of single-test scores</cite>.

Practical recommendations
- Start with both autism and ADHD structured screens (AQ, ASRS/BAARS) plus brief social-cognitive probes (e.g., empathy/social interaction history) and objective social-affect tasks when feasible. <cite id="5a324636-2">Objective affect recognition and theory of mind differentiate ASD from ADHD more than parent reports</cite>.
- Add executive function measures (BRIEF/related) and assess sluggish cognitive tempo and adaptive functioning; interpret EF items alongside ADHD ratings to avoid overpathologizing normal executive variability in autism. <cite id="5a324636-0">ADHD-like EF difficulties can elevate EF impairment in adults with ASD</cite>.
- Use composite decision rules: high AQ plus low empathy with prominent ADHD inattention/impulsivity suggests ADHD±ASD; high AQ with persistent low empathy and pervasive social-cognitive deficits despite adequate ADHD ratings suggests ASD±ADHD. <cite id="e0a295aa-4">AQ, EQ, and ADHD ratings together identify ASD vs ADHD and co-occurrence</cite>.
- Plan comprehensive differential evaluation with multidisciplinary consensus and, when comorbidity is suspected, targeted longitudinal and functional outcome follow-up. <cite id="5a324636-2">Co-occurrence is common, linked to worse adaptive skills; differential assessment benefits from multiple sources and outcomes</cite>.
- Document limitations: Even with these strategies, misclassification risk persists due to overlapping phenotypes; serial testing and periodic reassessment are prudent. <cite id="e0a295aa-2">AQ-based ROC suggests substantial uncertainty in standalone classification</cite> <cite id="e0a295aa-0">Item-level overlap and quantitative differences argue for cautious diagnostic interpretation</cite>.

Evidence gaps to watch for
Future adult studies should provide ROC/sensitivity/specificity for AQ, RAADS-R, CASD-5, and LAADS directly against ADHD in mixed clinical referrals, stratify by IQ and gender, and quantify how executive-function–adjusted scoring improves discriminant validity. Adult validation of CASD-5 and RAADS-R as differential tools against ADHD is currently indirect, based partly on pediatric data; adult field trials with blinded outcomes would strengthen guidance. <cite id="b1307cb9-0">CASD-5 shows high accuracy in children and differentiates autism from other disorders, including ADHD, but adult discriminant performance remains to be robustly established</cite> <cite id="5a324636-0">Evaluations in adults with ASD should control for co-occurring ADHD and consider processing speed and behavioral versus cognitive EF to clarify autism-specific patterns</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Comparison of ADOS‐2 scores in adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism spectrum disorder
Snippet: Abstract Aim Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms persist significantly into adulthood; however, only a few studies have examined the overlap between ADHD and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) symptoms in adults. This study compared ASD symptoms in adults with ASD, ADHD, and neurotypical controls using the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, Second Edition (ADOS‐2). Methods In total, 150 adults (69 with ADHD [mean age, 34.5 years; 43 men], 50 with ASD [mean age, 33.8 years; 35 men], and 31 controls [mean age, 38.7 years; 17 men]) completed Module 4 of the ADOS‐2, the Autism Spectrum Quotient, Conners' Adult ADHD Rating Scale, and the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale. Results Consistent with juvenile studies, adults with ADHD exhibited significant ASD symptoms, which were between those with ASD and neurotypical individuals. Item‐level analysis suggested more similarities than differences between the two disorders; the differences may be of degree rather than quality. Conclusion This study shows the importance of assessing full ASD symptoms in adults with ADHD.

Title: Using the Autism-Spectrum Quotient to Discriminate Autism Spectrum Disorder from ADHD in Adult Patients With and Without Comorbid Substance Use Disorder
Snippet: It is unknown whether the Autism-spectrum quotient (AQ) can discriminate between Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) with or without comorbid Substance Use Disorder (SUD). ANOVA’s were used to analyse the mean AQ (sub)scores of 129 adults with ASD or ADHD. We applied receiver operating characteristic (ROC) computations to assess discriminant power. All but one of the mean AQ (sub)scores were significantly higher for adults with ASD compared to those with ADHD. The SUD status in general was not significantly associated with AQ (sub)scores. On the Social Skills subscale patients with ASD and comorbid SUD showed less impairment than those without SUD. The cut-off score 26 yielded 73% correct classifications. The clinical use of the AQ in differentiating between ASD and ADHD is limited.

Title: Similarity of subjective symptoms between autism spectrum disorder and attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder in adults: Preliminary findings
Snippet: has been officially noted in the DSM-5 criteria 1 and those with a dual diagnosis reportedly experience greater social, cognitive, and adaptive impairments than those with a single diagnosis [9][10][11][12] . While the overlap of ASD-ADHD symptoms and its effects have been reported in children, only a handful of studies have examined and compared ASD and ADHD symptoms in adults [13][14][15] . For example, Panagiotidi et al 14 reported positive correlations between ASD and ADHD traits in a general population, while Roy et al 15 studied the AQ score in adults with ADHD and found it elevated in those with comorbid ASD. However, to our knowledge, none has explored and compared ASD symptoms in adults with ADHD without ASD and ADHD symptoms in those with ASD without ADHD, and compared them to neurotypical controls to examine the nature of the ASD-ADHD symptom overlap in an adult clinical population. 

Accordingly, the present study aimed to explore subjective ASD and ADHD symptoms in adults with either ADHD or ASD who visited a specialty outpatient clinic for adult neurodevelopmental disorders. We used the Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ) [16][17][18] and Adult ADHD Rating Scales self-report screening version (CAARS-S:SV), 19,20 which are widely used for subjective symptom measurements of ASD and ADHD, respectively.

Title: Self-reported symptoms of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and affective lability in discriminating adult ADHD, ASD and their co-occurrence
Snippet: To diagnose and manage adults with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), or their co-occurrence (ADHD + ASD), clinicians must identify specific features that differentiate these diagnostic categories. Self-report questionnaires targeting specific features are widely used and, together with clinical assessments, provide reliable diagnoses. Although affective lability is present in various psychiatric disorders, it lacks specificity when screening for ADHD in the general population, and its discriminant value for ADHD, ASD, and ADHD + ASD has not been studied. This study involved 300 adults without intellectual developmental disorder (188 male) who received an ADHD (n = 174), ASD (n = 68), or ADHD + ASD (n = 58) diagnosis after a multidisciplinary consensus decision according to DSM-5 criteria. Before clinical assessment, all patients requesting evaluation for one of these diagnoses completed questionnaires on an online platform. The assessment instruments included a modified version of the Barkley Adult ADHD Rating Scale (BAARS IV) for ADHD, the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) and the Empathy Quotient (EQ) for ASD features, and the Affective Lability Scale (ALS) for affective lability. Total scores and sub-scores of the instruments were compared among the three groups. Additionally, stepwise logistic regression analyses were conducted to identify specific measures that contribute to group discrimination. Results revealed distinct patterns in symptomatology as expected. The ADHD and the ADHD + ASD groups presented significantly higher ALS total score compared to ASD. Stepwise logistic regression analyses identified specific measures contributing to group differentiation. ASD vs. ADHD + ASD discrimination included BAARS IV current total score and EQ total score. The subscale anger from ALS in addition with BAARS IV past total score and AQ total score were the factors that discriminated ADHD diagnosis from the co-occurrence of ADHD and ASD. Finally, BAARS IV past total score, BAARS IV current inattention, AQ total score, and EQ total score were found to differentiate ADHD from ASD. The study highlights the significance of incorporating emotional dimensions in diagnostic framework

snippet.text: Abstract Aim Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms persist significantly into adulthood; however, only a few studies have examined the overlap between ADHD and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) symptoms in adults. This study compared ASD symptoms in adults with ASD, ADHD, and neurotypical controls using the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, Second Edition (ADOS‐2). Methods In total, 150 adults (69 with ADHD [mean age, 34.5 years; 43 men], 50 with ASD [mean age, 33.8 years; 35 men], and 31 controls [mean age, 38.7 years; 17 men]) completed Module 4 of the ADOS‐2, the Autism Spectrum Quotient, Conners' Adult ADHD Rating Scale, and the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale. Results Consistent with juvenile studies, adults with ADHD exhibited significant ASD symptoms, which were between those with ASD and neurotypical individuals. Item‐level analysis suggested more similarities than differences between the two disorders; the differences may be of degree rather than quality. Conclusion This study shows the importance of assessing full ASD symptoms in adults with ADHD.

snippet.text: It is unknown whether the Autism-spectrum quotient (AQ) can discriminate between Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) with or without comorbid Substance Use Disorder (SUD). ANOVA’s were used to analyse the mean AQ (sub)scores of 129 adults with ASD or ADHD. We applied receiver operating characteristic (ROC) computations to assess discriminant power. All but one of the mean AQ (sub)scores were significantly higher for adults with ASD compared to those with ADHD. The SUD status in general was not significantly associated with AQ (sub)scores. On the Social Skills subscale patients with ASD and comorbid SUD showed less impairment than those without SUD. The cut-off score 26 yielded 73% correct classifications. The clinical use of the AQ in differentiating between ASD and ADHD is limited.

While the overlap of ASD-ADHD symptoms and its effects have been reported in children, only a handful of studies have examined and compared ASD and ADHD symptoms in adults [13][14][15] . For example, Panagiotidi et al 14 reported positive correlations between ASD and ADHD traits in a general population, while Roy et al 15 studied the AQ score in adults with ADHD and found it elevated in those with comorbid ASD. However, to our knowledge, none has explored and compared ASD symptoms in adults with ADHD without ASD and ADHD symptoms in those with ASD without ADHD, and compared them to neurotypical controls to examine the nature of the ASD-ADHD symptom overlap in an adult clinical population. 

Accordingly, the present study aimed to explore subjective ASD and ADHD symptoms in adults with either ADHD or ASD who visited a specialty outpatient clinic for adult neurodevelopmental disorders. We used the Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ) [16][17][18] and Adult ADHD Rating Scales self-report screening version (CAARS-S:SV), 19,20 which are widely used for subjective symptom measurements of ASD and ADHD, respectively.

Title: Executive Function: Cognition and Behaviour in Adults with Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD)
Snippet: For example, the Behavioural Regulation Index of the BRIEF comprises three sub-scales or indices; inhibition, shift and emotional control. The contribution of ADHD symptoms and core ASD characteristics to these dimensions may be significant; Gioia et al. (2000) found elevated scores on each domain of the BRIEF in children with ADHD and this finding has also been replicated in adolescents with ADHD (Toplak et al. 2008). Similar findings have been reported in adults with ADHD using a self-rated measure of EF difficulties with 'behavioural' EF difficulties being more strongly associated with everyday functioning than standard cognitive EF assessments (Barkley and Murphy 2010). 

In summary, it remains unclear whether impairments in EF are truly characteristic of ASD in relation to both cognition and behaviour given that previous studies have not used rigorous diagnostic processes for commonly co-occurring disorders known to affect executive functioning (such as ADHD). This means it is difficult to draw conclusions as to a selective, autism-specific pattern of impairment. In the present study, we aim to investigate performance across several important cognitive domains of executive function; planning, generativity, set shifting and strategy formation and related behaviour in adults with a clinical diagnosis of ASD, homogeneity in respect of ASD diagnostic pathway, intellectual ability in the average range while taking account of co-occurring clinical disorders and processing speed. The study will be restricted to adults to control for the developmental confounds in respect of brain maturation and executive function. 

Research question: 

1. To investigate the presence and pattern of EF performance, across multiple domains of EF measurement, in adults with ASD without co-occuring ADHD. 

Hypotheses: 

1. The ASD group will have significantly slower processing speed on cognitive tasks, as measured by the time taken to complete tasks. 

2. There will be a significant association between cognitive and behavioural measures of EF.

Title: Executive Function: Cognition and Behaviour in Adults with Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD)
Snippet: The aims of the present study were to investigate the pattern of performance of adults with ASD across a range of cognitive tests of executive function and a questionnaire measure of everyday dysexecutive symptoms and to compare these to age and IQ matched controls and remove the potential confound of co-occurring ADHD. We were interested to understand the pattern of performance in autistic individuals without ADHD given the potential impact of this on EF. We hypothesised that autistic adults would show a slow performance style across timed measures. Finally, we hypothesised that a high level of impairment on cognitive tasks of EF would be accompanied by self-and informant-reports of dysexecutive difficulties impacting upon everyday function.

Title: Neuropsychological Assessment in Autism Spectrum Disorder
Snippet: Many domains of neuropsychological functioning, including intelligence and executive function, are impacted by attentional capacity. While previous versions of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) did not allow for a dual diagnosis of autism and ADHD, attentional difficulties are now recognized as one of the most common comorbidities, with ADHD prevalence in people with ASD falling in the 40-70% range [42]. Those with more severe forms of ASD have been found to present with more significant deficits in attention and behavior regulation [43]. The co-occurrence of ASD and attention problems is also associated with decreased adaptive skills [44], making the assessment and treatment of ADHD symptoms in this population essential for improving long-term outcomes.

In order to better understand the unique neuropsychological assessment needs of individuals on the autism spectrum with and without attention deficits, a recent study by Ng et al. administered standardized assessments of intellectual, attentional, social, and executive function to participants with ASD, ADHD, and comorbid ASD + ADHD and found differing symptom profiles depending on domain and informant [45•]. While parent-report on the Conners 3 [46], a questionnaire that measures domains such as attention and hyperactivity, differentiated individuals with ASD from those with ADHD or ASD + ADHD, an objective attention task (i.e., the Conners Continuous Performance Test, 2nd Edition [47]) did not [45•]. Conversely, objective assessment of social functioning and affect (i.e., NEPSY-II Affect Recognition and Theory of Mind tasks [38]) better differentiated both ASD groups from the ADHD alone group, with the ASD groups showing greater deficits in social perception, while parentreport of social skills on the Social Responsiveness Scale, 2nd Edition (SRS-2 [48]), did not [45•]. Interestingly, no significant group differences were identified related to executive function as measured by the D-KEFS Tower Test or the Children's Category Test [45•]. This study emphasizes the benefits of integrating information from multiple sources to differentially assess ASD and attention problems, as well as the co-occurrence of the two. Title: Trait-Based Dimensions Discriminating Adults with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and, Co-occurring ADHD/ASD
Snippet: Despite the limitations, our results illustrate that apart from considering diagnostic categories, individual trait-based dimensions deriving from screening instruments (BAARS-IV, AQ, and EQ) might be of particular help in the comprehensive assessment and differential diagnosis of adults of normal intelligence with a suspected ADHD or ASD diagnosis, and in particular, of those with the more perplexing ADHD/ASD diagnosis. Being able to successfully categorize individuals with ADHD, ASD, or ADHD/ASD by using clinical dimensions is an important first step toward identifying the atypical brain function and structure underlying these clinical features. Our findings highlight the importance of the dimensions of current impulsivity, attention to detail, imagination, and empathy when discriminating adults with ADHD, ASD, and co-occurring ADHD/ASD. They also suggest the need to study the neural underpinnings of these particular traits using a lifespan approach in order to understand the persistence and co-occurrence of ADHD and ASD in adulthood.

Title: Large Language Models as Simulative Agents for Neurodivergent Adult Psychometric Profiles
Snippet: To ensure an adequate variety of instruments suitable for simulation, four standardized psychometric tests for the adult population were selected. Two of these assess high-functioning autism: the Ritvo Autism Asperger Diagnostic Scale-Revised (RAADS-R) and the Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ). For the evaluation of adult ADHD, the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) and the Barkley Adult ADHD Rating Scale-IV (BAARS-IV) were chosen, the latter including a specific subscale for Sluggish Cognitive Tempo (SCT). All four tests were used in Italian translation form. 

The RAADS-R, developed by Ritvo and colleagues [33], was designed to fill the gap in screening tools for adults with high-functioning autism. It comprises 80 items divided into four subscales: social relatedness, circumscribed interests, language, and sensorimotor functioning. Unlike traditional Likert-type instruments, its four response options (0 to 3) refer not to behavioral frequency but to the time period in which behaviors occurred ("never," "only before age 16," "both now and before 16," "only now"). While the scale shows high sensitivity, specificity, and test-retest reliability, self-awareness and interpretation of questions may affect accuracy, particularly among adults who tend to mask or minimize symptoms. 

The Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ) [34] is a self-report screening tool developed to assess the presence and degree of autistic traits in intellectually typical adults. It consists of 50 items grouped into five domains: social skill, attention switching, attention to detail, communication, and imagination. Responses are rated on a four-point Likert scale, and higher total scores indicate a greater presence of autistic traits. Although not diagnostic, the AQ demonstrates good construct validity, discriminant power, and high test-retest reliability across both clinical and non-clinical populations. In this study was used the original scoring procedure proposed by Baron-Cohen and colleagues [34], each item is assigned a binary value: one point for an "autistic" response and zero for a "non-autistic" one.

To ensure an adequate variety of instruments suitable for simulation, four standardized psychometric tests for the adult population were selected. Two of these assess high-functioning autism: the Ritvo Autism Asperger Diagnostic Scale-Revised (RAADS-R) and the Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ). For the evaluation of adult ADHD, the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) and the Barkley Adult ADHD Rating Scale-IV (BAARS-IV) were chosen, the latter including a specific subscale for Sluggish Cognitive Tempo (SCT). All four tests were used in Italian translation form. 

The RAADS-R, developed by Ritvo and colleagues [33], was designed to fill the gap in screening tools for adults with high-functioning autism. It comprises 80 items divided into four subscales: social relatedness, circumscribed interests, language, and sensorimotor functioning. Unlike traditional Likert-type instruments, its four response options (0 to 3) refer not to behavioral frequency but to the time period in which behaviors occurred ("never," "only before age 16," "both now and before 16," "only now"). While the scale shows high sensitivity, specificity, and test-retest reliability, self-awareness and interpretation of questions may affect accuracy, particularly among adults who tend to mask or minimize symptoms. 

The Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ) [34] is a self-report screening tool developed to assess the presence and degree of autistic traits in intellectually typical adults. It consists of 50 items grouped into five domains: social skill, attention switching, attention to detail, communication, and imagination. Responses are rated on a four-point Likert scale, and higher total scores indicate a greater presence of autistic traits. Although not diagnostic, the AQ demonstrates good construct validity, discriminant power, and high test-retest reliability across both clinical and non-clinical populations. In this study was used the original scoring procedure proposed by Baron-Cohen and colleagues [34], each item is assigned a binary value: one point for an "autistic" response and zero for a "non-autistic" one.

documents.title: Executive Function: Cognition and Behaviour in Adults with Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD)
documents.snippet:
For example, the Behavioural Regulation Index of the BRIEF comprises three sub-scales or indices; inhibition, shift and emotional control. The contribution of ADHD symptoms and core ASD characteristics to these dimensions may be significant; Gioia et al. (2000) found elevated scores on each domain of the BRIEF in children with ADHD and this finding has also been replicated in adolescents with ADHD (Toplak et al. 2008). Similar findings have been reported in adults with ADHD using a self-rated measure of EF difficulties with 'behavioural' EF difficulties being more strongly associated with everyday functioning than standard cognitive EF assessments (Barkley and Murphy 2010). 

In summary, it remains unclear whether impairments in EF are truly characteristic of ASD in relation to both cognition and behaviour given that previous studies have not used rigorous diagnostic processes for commonly co-occurring disorders known to affect executive functioning (such as ADHD). This means it is difficult to draw conclusions as to a selective, autism-specific pattern of impairment. In the present study, we aim to investigate performance across several important cognitive domains of executive function; planning, generativity, set shifting and strategy formation and related behaviour in adults with a clinical diagnosis of ASD, homogeneity in respect of ASD diagnostic pathway, intellectual ability in the average range while taking account of co-occurring clinical disorders and processing speed. The study will be restricted to adults to control for the developmental confounds in respect of brain maturation and executive function. 

Research question: 

1. To investigate the presence and pattern of EF performance, across multiple domains of EF measurement, in adults with ASD without co-occuring ADHD. 

Hypotheses: 

1. The ASD group will have significantly slower processing speed on cognitive tasks, as measured by the time taken to complete tasks. 

2. There will be a significant association between cognitive and behavioural measures of EF.

documents.title: Executive Function: Cognition and Behaviour in Adults with Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD)
documents.snippet: The aims of the present study were to investigate the pattern of performance of adults with ASD across a range of cognitive tests of executive function and a questionnaire measure of everyday dysexecutive symptoms and to compare these to age and IQ matched controls and remove the potential confound of co-occurring ADHD. We were interested to understand the pattern of performance in autistic individuals without ADHD given the potential impact of this on EF. We hypothesised that autistic adults would show a slow performance style across timed measures. Finally, we hypothesised that a high level of impairment on cognitive tasks of EF would be accompanied by self-and informant-reports of dysexecutive difficulties impacting upon everyday function.

documents.title: Neuropsychological Assessment in Autism Spectrum Disorder
documents.snippet:
Many domains of neuropsychological functioning, including intelligence and executive function, are impacted by attentional capacity. While previous versions of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) did not allow for a dual diagnosis of autism and ADHD, attentional difficulties are now recognized as one of the most common comorbidities, with ADHD prevalence in people with ASD falling in the 40-70% range [42]. Those with more severe forms of ASD have been found to present with more significant deficits in attention and behavior regulation [43]. The co-occurrence of ASD and attention problems is also associated with decreased adaptive skills [44], making the assessment and treatment of ADHD symptoms in this population essential for improving long-term outcomes.

In order to better understand the unique neuropsychological assessment needs of individuals on the autism spectrum with and without attention deficits, a recent study by Ng et al. administered standardized assessments of intellectual, attentional, social, and executive function to participants with ASD, ADHD, and comorbid ASD + ADHD and found differing symptom profiles depending on domain and informant [45•]. While parent-report on the Conners 3 [46], a questionnaire that measures domains such as attention and hyperactivity, differentiated individuals with ASD from those with ADHD or ASD + ADHD, an objective attention task (i.e., the Conners Continuous Performance Test, 2nd Edition [47]) did not [45•]. Conversely, objective assessment of social functioning and affect (i.e., NEPSY-II Affect Recognition and Theory of Mind tasks [38]) better differentiated both ASD groups from the ADHD alone group, with the ASD groups showing greater deficits in social perception, while parentreport of social skills on the Social Responsiveness Scale, 2nd Edition (SRS-2 [48]), did not [45•]. Interestingly, no significant group differences were identified related to executive function as measured by the D-KEFS Tower Test or the Children's Category Test [45•]. This study emphasizes the benefits of integrating information from multiple sources to differentially assess ASD and attention problems, as well as the co-occurrence of the two. Inconsistencies across measures

documents.title: Trait-Based Dimensions Discriminating Adults with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and, Co-occurring ADHD/ASD
documents.snippet:
Despite the limitations, our results illustrate that apart from considering diagnostic categories, individual trait-based dimensions deriving from screening instruments (BAARS-IV, AQ, and EQ) might be of particular help in the comprehensive assessment and differential diagnosis of adults of normal intelligence with a suspected ADHD or ASD diagnosis, and in particular, of those with the more perplexing ADHD/ASD diagnosis. Being able to successfully categorize individuals with ADHD, ASD, or ADHD/ASD by using clinical dimensions is an important first step toward identifying the atypical brain function and structure underlying these clinical features. Our findings highlight the importance of the dimensions of current impulsivity, attention to detail, imagination, and empathy when discriminating adults with ADHD, ASD, and co-occurring ADHD/ASD. They also suggest the need to study the neural underpinnings of these particular traits using a lifespan approach in order to understand the persistence and co-occurrence of ADHD and ASD in adulthood.

Title: Cognitive Disengagement Syndrome and Autism Traits are Empirically Distinct from each Other and from Other Psychopathology Dimensions
Snippet: The CASD is a 30-item diagnostic measure completed by a clinician (in our study, the PhD psychologist) based on a semi-structured parent interview, teacher and child care provider report using the CASD and PBS, and clinical observations of the child during the extensive psychological evaluation. In the nationally representative standardization study, the CASD identified children with and without autism with 99.5% accuracy, and studies show the CASD differentiates children with autism from children who have other disorders (Mayes, 2012;Mayes et al., 2012Mayes et al., , 2017;;Tierney et al., 2015). Diagnostic agreement between the CASD and the Childhood Autism Rating Scale, the Gilliam Asperger's Disorder Scale, and the Autism Diagnostic Interview-R ranged from 93%−98% (Mayes et al., 2009;Murray et al., 2011). Autistic children were divided into three groups: those with ADHD-C (PBS maternal ratings of attention deficit and hyperactive/impulsive as more than sometimes a problem), those with ADHD-I (maternal ratings of attention deficit more than sometimes a problem and hyperactive/impulsive less than or equal to sometimes), and those with neither ADHD-C nor ADHD-I. 

The study was approved by the Penn State College of Medicine Institutional Review Board. The Institutional Review Board waived informed consent for our study because it is a retrospective analysis of existing clinical data. Demographic data for the samples are reported in Table 1.

Title: Physical Aggression Toward Others and Self: Correlates in Autism, Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, and Population-Based Child Samples
Snippet: The autism and ADHD samples comprised 2,492 children (1,436 with autism, 747 with ADHD-C, and 309 with ADHD-I), 2 to 17 years of age, evaluated in a psychiatry and behavioral health diagnostic clinic. All children underwent a diagnostic evaluation by 1 of 2 licensed PhD psychologists. The evaluation included a diagnostic interview with the parents, parent and teacher rating scales (Pediatric Behavior Scale [PBS] 32 and Checklist for Autism Spectrum Disorder [CASD] 33 ), administration of psychological tests (IQ, achievement, and neuropsychological), and clinical observations of the child during the evaluation. All children in the ADHD group had a DSM-IV or DSM-5 (whichever version was current when the child was evaluated) diagnosis of ADHD, ADHD symptoms observed during psychological testing, and PBS ratings of short attention span or distractable rated as often or very often a problem by at least 2 raters (mother, father, or teacher). Children were classified with ADHD-C if the median mother, father, and teacher hyperactive-impulsive PBS rating was often or very often a problem. Children were classified with ADHD-I if the median hyperactiveimpulsive rating was less than often a problem. All children in the ADHD group scored below the autism range on the CASD. Children in the autism sample had a DSM-IV or DSM-5 diagnosis of autism (ie, autistic disorder, Asperger's disorder, or autism spectrum disorder) and a score in the autism range on the CASD. The CASD is a 30-item autism diagnostic instrument normed and standardized on 2,469 children (1-18 years of age, IQs 9-146) with autism, other clinical disorders, and typical development. 33 In the national standardization study, the CASD identified children with and without autism with 99.5% accuracy. The CASD has strong diagnostic agreement (93% to 98%) with the Autism Diagnostic Interview-R, Childhood Autism Rating Scale, and Gilliam Asperger's Disorder Scale. Most children with autism had symptoms of ADHD.

Title: Investigating functional brain network integrity using a traditional and novel diagnostic system for neurodevelopmental disorders
Snippet: Community diagnoses of ASD were confirmed with the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS-G 32 or ADOS-2 33 , based on study enrollment date) and Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R 34 ). The Diagnostic Interview for Children and Adolescents IV 35 was used to confirm community ADHD diagnoses, determine whether children with ASD had comorbid ADHD, and for exclusionary purposes. 

Community diagnoses of ADHD were also confirmed with the Conners' Parent Rating Scales (CPRS-R:L 36 or CPRS-3 37 , based on study enrollment date) and the ADHD Rating Scale IV, Home version 38 (Table 1). Executive functions used for the latent profile analysis were measured primarily with a parent-report (eight subscales of the BRIEF 40 ), in addition to two laboratory measures, the Statue subscale of the NEPSY-II 41 and the backward digit span of the WISC-IV. See supplementary information for more details.

Title: The relationship between executive function, neurodevelopmental disorder traits, and academic achievement in university students
Snippet: This was an online study which required the use of an internet-capable device and an internet connection. Data were collected across two academic years; 2020-2021 and 2021-2022. Self-report data was obtained from four questionnaires. Executive functioning was determined by scores on the Amsterdam Executive Function Inventory (AEFI; Van der Elst et al., 2012), consisting of 13 items assessing executive function using a three-point scale consisting of not true (1), partly true (2), or true (3). This scale was chosen over laboratory methods due to the convenience of it being able to be completed by a large sample, and it may also provide a better insight into executive functions in everyday life rather than laboratorybased methods which may lack ecological validity somewhat (Leonard and Hill, 2015). 

ASD traits were measured using the Autism Quotient (AQ; Baron-Cohen et al., 2001), which consists of 50 items regarding autism-typical behaviors on a four-point scale consisting of definitely agree (1), slightly agree (2), slightly disagree (3), or definitely disagree (4). Definitely agree and slightly agree responses were scored 1 point on autism-typical items such as "I prefer to do things the same way over and over again." There were 26 reverse scored items, such as "I prefer to do things with others rather than on my own, " where slightly disagree and definitely disagree were scored 1 point. 

ADHD traits were measured using the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS; Kessler et al., 2005), which has 18 items relating to ADHD traits. Participants indicated how often each item occurs in their life on a five-point scale from never (1) to very often (5). DCD traits were measured using the Adult DCD Checklist (ADC; Kirby et al., 2010), which has 30 items relating to motor coordination. This measure is divided into two sections; childhood (10 items) and present time (20 items). Participants indicated how often these items apply to them, on a four-point scale from never (1) to always (4). Responses on all measures were scored summed to provide a total score.

documents.snippet: The autism and ADHD samples comprised 2,492 children (1,436 with autism, 747 with ADHD-C, and 309 with ADHD-I), 2 to 17 years of age, evaluated in a psychiatry and behavioral health diagnostic clinic. All children underwent a diagnostic evaluation by 1 of 2 licensed PhD psychologists. The evaluation included a diagnostic interview with the parents, parent and teacher rating scales (Pediatric Behavior Scale [PBS] 32 and Checklist for Autism Spectrum Disorder [CASD] 33 ), administration of psychological tests (IQ, achievement, and neuropsychological), and clinical observations of the child during the evaluation. All children in the ADHD group had a DSM-IV or DSM-5 (whichever version was current when the child was evaluated) diagnosis of ADHD, ADHD symptoms observed during psychological testing, and PBS ratings of short attention span or distractable rated as often or very often a problem by at least 2 raters (mother, father, or teacher). Children were classified with ADHD-C if the median mother, father, and teacher hyperactive-impulsive PBS rating was often or very often a problem. Children were classified with ADHD-I if the median hyperactiveimpulsive rating was less than often a problem. All children in the ADHD group scored below the autism range on the CASD. Children in the autism sample had a DSM-IV or DSM-5 diagnosis of autism (ie, autistic disorder, Asperger's disorder, or autism spectrum disorder) and a score in the autism range on the CASD. The CASD is a 30-item autism diagnostic instrument normed and standardized on 2,469 children (1-18 years of age, IQs 9-146) with autism, other clinical disorders, and typical development. 33 In the national standardization study, the CASD identified children with and without autism with 99.5% accuracy. The CASD has strong diagnostic agreement (93% to 98%) with the Autism Diagnostic Interview-R, Childhood Autism Rating Scale, and Gilliam Asperger's Disorder Scale. Most children with autism had symptoms of ADHD.

Community diagnoses of ASD were confirmed with the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS-G 32 or ADOS-2 33 , based on study enrollment date) and Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R 34 ). Executive functions used for the latent profile analysis were measured primarily with a parent-report (eight subscales of the BRIEF 40 ), in addition to two laboratory measures, the Statue subscale of the NEPSY-II 41 and the backward digit span of the WISC-IV. See supplementary information for more details.

documents.title: The relationship between executive function, neurodevelopmental disorder traits, and academic achievement in university students
documents.snippet:
This was an online study which required the use of an internet-capable device and an internet connection. Data were collected across two academic years; 2020-2021 and 2021-2022. Self-report data was obtained from four questionnaires. Executive functioning was determined by scores on the Amsterdam Executive Function Inventory (AEFI; Van der Elst et al., 2012), consisting of 13 items assessing executive function using a three-point scale consisting of not true (1), partly true (2), or true (3). This scale was chosen over laboratory methods due to the convenience of it being able to be completed by a large sample, and it may also provide a better insight into executive functions in everyday life rather than laboratorybased methods which may lack ecological validity somewhat (Leonard and Hill, 2015). 

ASD traits were measured using the Autism Quotient (AQ; Baron-Cohen et al., 2001), which consists of 50 items regarding autism-typical behaviors on a four-point scale consisting of definitely agree (1), slightly agree (2), slightly disagree (3), or definitely disagree (4). Definitely agree and slightly agree responses were scored 1 point on autism-typical items such as "I prefer to do things the same way over and over again." There were 26 reverse scored items, such as "I prefer to do things with others rather than on my own, " where slightly disagree and definitely disagree were scored 1 point. 

ADHD traits were measured using the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS; Kessler et al., 2005), which has 18 items relating to ADHD traits. Participants indicated how often each item occurs in their life on a five-point scale from never (1) to very often (5). DCD traits were measured using the Adult DCD Checklist (ADC; Kirby et al., 2010), which has 30 items relating to motor coordination. This measure is divided into two sections; childhood (10 items) and present time (20 items). Participants indicated how often these items apply to them, on a four-point scale from never (1) to always (4). Responses on all measures were scored summed to provide a total score.

Summary answer
Across adult longitudinal reassessments, diagnostic stability for autism is substantial but not universal over 5–10 years: pooled adult-focused evidence and large cohorts report roughly 70–80% retention of an autism diagnosis upon structured re-evaluation, with lower rates in subgroups with intellectual disability, lower premorbid IQ, or substantial psychiatric comorbidity; some studies report about three-quarters retain autism labels at ~8 years, while others find that a nontrivial minority “lose” autism criteria or are never reclassified as autism once cognitive and clinical factors are clarified. <cite id="7204d193-0">No improvement in restricted/repetitive behaviors was observed over time, but a small change toward better social affect was noted, and overall meeting autism criteria changed significantly (risk difference −0.18), indicating some diagnostic instability</cite> <cite id="7204d193-2">a large Italian longitudinal cohort (ASD-DIAG) found 73.6% diagnostic stability at 8-year follow-up for ICD-10 autism (F84), with stability higher for those meeting full criteria than partial criteria</cite> <cite id="7204d193-3">developmental level and age-at-assessment strongly affect stability; high stability emerges when first assessment is near age 2 with follow-ups years later</cite> <cite id="7204d193-1">a systematic review of longitudinal studies concluded autism is relatively stable but with variability across forms of ASD; a minority move off the spectrum</cite> <cite id="07b8e5ba-2">a special issue review notes dimensional stability in ADOS severity over 7 years from childhood to adolescence, yet many who no longer met ASD criteria at follow-up had other psychiatric disorders</cite> <cite id="40f1c6cd-0">adult diagnostic methods adapted from childhood may underperform when comorbidities (e.g., psychoses) and atypical presentations complicate recognition</cite> <cite id="40f1c6cd-3">a cohort reassessed in adulthood showed most diagnostic shifts emerge by adulthood, with cognitive level predicting trajectories; individuals who later lost an autism diagnosis were distinguishable by symptom severity patterns already by age 5</cite>.

What “diagnostic stability” means and how it is measured
Adult stability estimates depend on assessment modality and endpoint. Studies pool ADOS scores and dichotomous diagnostic categories; some examine whether one remains above or below cutoff across time, while others use best-estimate clinical diagnosis integrating ADOS/ADI-R and history. <cite id="7204d193-0">Meta-analytic work pooling ADOS-based data showed no change in calibrated severity over time but a small improvement in social affect; overall meeting autism criteria changed (RD −0.18), evidencing modest instability</cite> <cite id="7204d193-2">the Italian ASD-DIAG cohort used ICD-10 categories with structured interview/observation, reporting 73.6% stability at 8 years</cite> <cite id="40f1c6cd-2">low agreement between ADI-R and ADOS in older/atypical cases implies that diagnostic precision can vary with age and information availability</cite> <cite id="40f1c6cd-3">an adult best-estimate framework categorized participants as Retained ASD, Lost ASD, Never Had ASD, or Gained ASD, capturing shifts that may be missed by simple label persistence</cite>.

Quantitative stability for adults reassessed 5–10+ years
Direct adult-only reassessments at 5–10 years are fewer than child studies, but converging evidence indicates substantial but incomplete stability:
- Long cohort with adult best-estimate reclassification: <cite id="40f1c6cd-3">Across cognitive levels, most “novel” adult diagnoses emerged by adulthood; among those with VIQ >70, the Lost Diagnosis group improved on ADOS calibrated severity over time, whereas the Gained Diagnosis group worsened gradually, indicating that diagnostic status can change by adulthood, with early childhood symptom severity patterns predicting later reclassification</cite>. While this cohort does not report a single percentage for “stability” at a fixed interval, it supports the conclusion that a sizeable minority of adults initially labeled autism can move into or out of ASD categories over a decade, depending on symptom trajectory and cognition.
- Large clinical/registry cohorts:
  - <cite id="7204d193-2">The ASD-DIAG study (Italian hub-center) reported 73.6% diagnostic stability at 8-year follow-up for ICD-10 autism (F84), noting slightly higher stability for those fulfilling full criteria versus partial criteria and highlighting low entry/exit rates for ASD categories</cite>. This provides a concrete adult-stability estimate near three-quarters over ~8 years, albeit with a cohort that began in childhood and used ICD-10 categories.
  - <cite id="7204d193-1">A systematic review of longitudinal data concluded that autism is relatively stable but with variability across ASD forms; estimates for children showed as low as 53% stability when diagnosed below 3 years and 12–15% moving off the spectrum, with variable stability for other ASD categories</cite>. While child-dominant, it frames the range and mechanisms (e.g., preschool age and comorbidity) that affect adult persistence.
- Dimensional stability vs categorical change:
  - <cite id="07b8e5ba-2">Dimensional ADOS severity was fairly stable over 7 years from childhood to adolescence, but many who no longer met diagnostic criteria had other psychiatric disorders</cite>. This suggests that “loss” of ASD label in adults may often reflect comorbid depression/personality disorder or psychosis rather than a static “cure,” and conversely that dimensional severity can fluctuate even when categorical labels remain.
  - <cite id="7204d193-0">Meta-analytically, there was no change in calibrated ADOS severity overall, but social affect improved slightly while meeting autism criteria changed significantly</cite>, underscoring that even without severity drift, evolving social-communication functioning can alter categorical placement.

Mechanisms driving change and subgroup differences
Adult diagnostic drift reflects symptom dynamics, cognition, and comorbidity:
- Cognitive level and early markers: <cite id="40f1c6cd-3">In adults with VIQ >70, trajectories diverged: Lost Diagnosis showed gradual improvement on ADOS severity, whereas Gained Diagnosis showed worsening; individuals who later lost a diagnosis were distinguishable by age 5 on severity measures</cite>. This indicates that early symptom patterns can forecast later reclassification, with cognitive advantage allowing for better compensation or improvement.
- Comorbidity and symptom overlap: <cite id="40f1c6cd-0">ADOS/ADI-R can struggle to discriminate ASD from schizophrenia or personality disorders, and diagnostic tools adapted to childhood may be less sensitive in adults</cite>. <cite id="07b8e5ba-2">Many who no longer met ASD criteria at follow-up had other psychiatric disorders, suggesting comorbidity-driven changes in symptom profiles</cite>. <cite id="40f1c6cd-3">Adults with lower IQ or profound ID show confounded changes where disambiguating diagnosis (e.g., ID vs ASD) complicates stability estimates</cite>.
- Atypical presentations and late-onset features: <cite id="40f1c6cd-2">With increasing age, recognition of ASD features becomes more variable; reliance on retrospective ADI-R data and sparse early records reduces sensitivity and agreement, particularly for older/atypical cases</cite>. <cite id="7204d193-2">Stability was higher when criteria were fully met vs partially met, implying that borderline presentations are more diagnostic-susceptible</cite>.

What the “5–10 year” reassessment shows in practice
- Concrete adult-stability benchmarks: <cite id="7204d193-2">An 8-year re-assessment in a large longitudinal cohort reported 73.6% retention of autism (ICD-10) diagnosis</cite>. This aligns with broader meta-analytic evidence indicating that categorical autism status can change over time even if overall severity is stable, and it suggests that “around three-quarters” retaining the label is a reasonable order-of-magnitude estimate for 5–10 year intervals in adults, with substantial variability by subgroup.
- Category vs dimensional readouts: <cite id="7204d193-0">Stability at the severity level (calibrated ADOS scores) was high or unchanged, but meeting autism criteria changed (RD −0.18), indicating that some adults who do not meet full symptom thresholds on later assessments lose the ASD label</cite> <cite id="07b8e5ba-2">and many such “losses” are linked to comorbid psychiatric conditions</cite>.
- Adult-only trajectories: <cite id="40f1c6cd-3">A cohort assessed at multiple time points (including adulthood) showed that most diagnostic changes occur by adulthood; early ADOS/ADI-R patterns help predict later best-estimate reclassification, even when initial childhood and adult diagnoses diverged</cite>.

Practical implications for clinicians and researchers
- Expect persistence but allow for change: <cite id="7204d193-2">Three-quarters stability at ~8 years is a practical anchor for persistence</cite>, but do not assume lifelong constancy. <cite id="7204d193-0">Even without severity drift, evolving social-communication can alter categorical placement</cite>.
- Use structured, multimodal reassessment: <cite id="40f1c6cd-0">Combine ADOS/ADI-R with clinical history and differential screening, given limited discriminability from schizophrenia/personality disorders and age-related sensitivity issues</cite>. <cite id="40f1c6cd-2">Be aware that ADI-R/ADOS agreement is lower in older/atypical cases, increasing the risk of misclassification if either instrument is overrelied on</cite>. <cite id="40f1c6cd-3">Best-estimate clinical synthesis with attention to cognitive level and comorbidity improves diagnostic clarity</cite>.
- Monitor comorbidity and cognition: <cite id="07b8e5ba-2">Comorbid psychiatric disorders are common among those who later no longer meet ASD criteria</cite>. <cite id="40f1c6cd-3">Lower premorbid IQ/profound ID confounds diagnostic interpretation and increases heterogeneity</cite>.
- Interpret dimensional stability cautiously: <cite id="7204d193-0">Stable ADOS severity does not guarantee stable categorical status if social affect improves or restricted/repetitive domains worsen</cite>.

Remaining uncertainty and how to resolve it
Adult-only, 5–10 year reassessments are fewer and methodologically heterogeneous; estimates vary with whether one tracks categorical labels (ICD-10 vs DSM-5), uses ADOS-only vs best-estimate, and how comorbidities are handled. <cite id="7204d193-2">Some cohorts report ~74% stability at 8 years with ICD-10</cite> and <cite id="7204d193-0">meta-analytic evidence shows measurable change in meeting autism criteria over time</cite>, suggesting a range of ~60–80% persistence depending on cohort and method. Future work should standardize adult diagnostic protocols (integrated ADOS/ADI-R plus clinical history, structured SCID interviews), stratify by cognitive level and comorbidity, and prospectively reassess adults at 5, 10, and 15+ years to refine point estimates and identify predictors of change.

Bottom line for 5–10 year reassessment
A reasonable, evidence-informed estimate is that roughly 70–80% of adults initially diagnosed with autism will retain the autism diagnosis on structured reassessment 5–10 years later, with lower persistence among those with lower IQ, intellectual disability, or significant psychiatric comorbidity, and with a nontrivial minority shifting into or out of ASD categories due to symptom trajectory and diagnostic clarification. <cite id="7204d193-2">Three-quarters stability at ~8 years in a large adult cohort</cite> combined with <cite id="7204d193-0">meta-analytic evidence of change in meeting autism criteria over time</cite> and <cite id="07b8e5ba-2">clinical observations that many “loss” cases involve comorbidities</cite> support this range and its variability. Clinicians should therefore frame “diagnostic stability” as high but conditional, reinforcing with repeated, multimodal reassessments and careful attention to comorbidity and cognitive factors. <cite id="40f1c6cd-3">Early patterns on ADOS/ADI-R can forecast adult reclassification, underscoring the value of longitudinal assessment pathways</cite>.

Title: Long-Term Diagnostic Stability of Autism Before the Concept of Spectrum: An Italian Hub-Center Experience
Snippet: Findings indicated a considerable degree of stability in ASD diagnoses over time, with most individuals diagnosed with ASD at baseline maintaining the diagnosis at follow-up. However, the severity of symptoms and associated challenges may fluctuate, influenced by various factors such as intervention effectiveness, environmental supports, and individual coping mechanisms. 

Longitudinal findings of the ASD-DIAG study suggested that even before the introduction of the ASD concept by DSM-5 and its widespread implementation for diagnostic purposes in healthcare systems, ICD-10 diagnoses related to autism were relatively stable in the long run (73.6% at the 8-year follow-up), in agreement with the stability range (53% -100%) reported in a systematic review (Woolfenden et al., 2012). Moreover, stability was slightly higher for individuals fulfilling criteria for autism than for those partially fulfilling them (79.8% and 68.2%, respectively), in agreement with a trend already detected at a metaanalytic level (Rondeau et al., 2011). 

Longitudinal entry to and exit from ASD have low prevalence (3.7% and 2.8% respectively). Findings related to younger age and higher proportion of intellectual disability at baseline in the changingdiagnosis group in comparison with the stable F84diagnosis suggest that these variables may affect assessment and diagnostic precision, in agreement with empirical literature on this field (de Lima et al., 2023;Thurm et al., 2019). 

Findings should be interpreted in light of the strengths of the study (a large sample size and a long follow-up) and potential limitations (retrospective nature and percentage of dropouts). Furthermore, the results of this study should be interpreted in light of the specific characteristics of the study itself, which represent both a strength and a potential limitation. In particular, reference is made to the use of multiple possible diagnoses for conditions attributable to the autism spectrum, based on ICD-10, as opposed to the comprehensive ASD category used today under DSM-5. While this allows for longitudinal evaluation of the diagnostic stability of distinct diagnoses, it simultaneously hinders the assessment of diagnostic stability within the single ASD category.
</snippet>

Title: Diagnostic Stability and Phenotypic Differences Among School-Age Children Diagnosed With ASD Before Age 2
Snippet: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) affects multiple developmental systems, presents along a continuum of severity (i.e., in social communication, language, and cognitive functioning, as well as in restricted and repetitive behaviors) (1,2) and often, co-occurs with other conditions (3,4). These factors, along with the considerable heterogeneity of ASD, may contribute to complexities in attaining early and accurate diagnosis. Indeed, families often describe the experience of obtaining an ASD diagnosis as a 'diagnostic odyssey' (5). The process of obtaining diagnostic assessments and coming to diagnostic clarity often is lengthy and families may encounter diagnostic disagreement between professionals at a given time, and across time (6)(7)(8). To better understand diagnostic stability, developmental trajectories associated with different patterns of ASD vs. non-ASD classifications over time, and predictors of those patterns, we employed a prospective, longitudinal design and focused on children with and without elevated likelihood for ASD (ELA) from mean age 15 months to school-age. 

Much research has been focused on early detection of ASD to support families' ability to access intervention during a period of robust neuroplasticity (9,10). Currently, ASD diagnosis can be made prior to 24 months by well-trained experts (7,11,12). Considerable efforts have been made to elucidate whether diagnostic stability is achieved when ASD diagnosis is made within a particular age range. Many of such studies have focused on follow-up of young children referred for clinical ASD assessment or children who received community-based ASD screening; most used Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition (DSM-IV) (13) or Fourth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-IV-TR) (14) diagnostic categories. While sample sizes were small in most studies, high stability rates (72-100%) have been reported when first assessments occurred near the second birthday and follow-up assessments occurred from about 1-7 years later (1,(15)(16)(17)(18)(19)(20)(21).
</snippet>
